body.text: The state of play in Victoria's election as early voting kicks off
As election day in Victoria rapidly approaches, support for the Labor state government in opinion polling looks to have turned from bad to diabolical.
The big question hanging over the election for most of this year was whether anyone could win it outright and govern in majority.
In June and July, we had Labor, the Liberals and One Nation all polling first preferences in the mid-20s.
It suggested an extraordinarily complex result where One Nation was hovering near a tipping point where it could sweep a large number of seats.
When you combine that with the Greens' competitiveness in inner Melbourne, it looked like the government would be defending its seats against three different parties across the state's 88 districts.
Beside that was the sideshow of the Coalition, campaigning for majority government but pitted in direct competition for many seats with One Nation.
At the point the polls were pointing at that scenario, then-premier Jacinta Allan was replaced. That doesn't seem to have halted the slide away from Labor.
Several pollsters have recorded strengthening Coalition support in recent weeks, with Labor and One Nation both sliding.

We are still likely to see a milder version of that scenario play out on election day, but the Carroll government's best hope of retaining power at this point appears to lie in there being a significant miss by pollsters.
The Coalition is now recording statewide support just above 30 per cent, and the gap between the Coalition and One Nation has been widening since June and July.
The average of the polls collected in November puts that gap at nearly 10 percentage points.
That is very important, because the Coalition's path to majority government gets very difficult if it falls into third place in many electorates.
The opposition will benefit from preferences from both Labor and One Nation voters, but it needs to stay in first or second place to be in a position to receive them.
Polls now suggest that will happen in far fewer seats than could've been the case mid-year.
That means that the likelihood of One Nation winning a huge number of seats and depriving Liberal leader Jess Wilson of a majority has also dropped.
It takes the sting out of Ben Carroll's warnings of the prospects of a Coalition government allied with Pauline Hanson's party.
Given the trend in polling, it even raises questions about whether the premier's negative campaigning has backfired by sending more soft voters toward the Liberals.
A poll conducted by Resolve for the Nine newspapers this month also found that more voters were comfortable with the idea of the Coalition governing with One Nation than were uncomfortable.
Voters felt much less comfortable about Labor governing with the Greens.
Labor could be heading for a rout
While the situation appears to have markedly improved for Jess Wilson, Labor is staring down the barrel of not just defeat but an absolute wipe-out.

There is the real prospect of the government coming third on primaries statewide, while two-party-preferred results of the last few weeks have consistently estimated the Coalition at 55 or 56 per cent, with Labor at 45 or 46.
These numbers are a blunt tool to analyse the seat-by-seat contest, but a 45-55 result is equivalent to a swing of roughly 10 percentage points since the 2022 election.
A uniform swing that large would see the Coalition win about 30 seats from Labor.

We don't expect to see a uniform swing, but 30 is well above the 16 gains the Coalition need for a majority, giving the opposition a large amount of breathing room and suggesting a Labor rout is a real possibility.

Labor might hold on to some of those seats and it could lose some of them to One Nation instead, especially in Melbourne's outer fringe seats including Sunbury and Bass and in rural seats like Eureka and Ripon.

In fact, where Labor would've hoped a few months ago that One Nation would be a thorn in the side of the Coalition, nabbing seats in regional areas, it seems now that the party is a bigger threat to the government.
Labor and Green voters (limited though their number may be) in regional Victoria are more likely to preference the Coalition over One Nation.
Because of that, One Nation probably needs to be beating the Nationals on primaries in order to stay in the lead once preferences are distributed.
But Liberal voters will most likely preference One Nation above Labor, as suggested by the opposition's how to vote card.
That's why it may be easier for One Nation to win Melbourne seats from Labor in this election, if it can beat the Liberal candidate and poll within spitting distance of Labor.
If that happens, this election could send chills up the spine of Labor MPs around the country and prove that Pauline Hanson is a threat to both sides of politics.
Coalition could rule in majority with record low vote
Even if One Nation doesn't win many seats, polling suggests we are going to see some records broken at the end of the month.
Labor could record the worst primary vote of any sitting government in Australia since at least World War II.
But at the same time, we might see the Coalition come to majority government from a record low vote.

Aside from the ACT's first ever election under self-determination, which had some particularly unique circumstances, the combined Labor-Coalition vote never dipped below 65 per cent in any Australian election between 1945 and 2025.
It fell to 56.5 per cent in South Australia in March, when One Nation recorded its best ever statewide vote.
Victorian voters may hand the major parties a new low watermark.
